_meta.purpose: The ergonomic layer — the body, before any room exists. This is the level Neufert works at: percentile body dimensions, reach envelopes, the space an activity occupies. Everything above it (space types, clearances, validation rules) is derived from these numbers rather than asserted independently, so changing a user group's reach propagates through every rule that depends on it.
_meta.provenance_policy: Seeded from freely citable sources. `neufert_ref` is an empty slot on every record for you to fill from your own copy of Architects' Data for internal verification. Do NOT paste Neufert tables here — this repository is meant to be shareable and the work is copyrighted. Cite the regulation or standard as the published source; use Neufert to catch what you forgot to model.
_meta.percentile_note: P5 is used for REACH (design for the shortest reach so everyone can reach) and P95 for CLEARANCE (design for the largest body so everyone fits). Using P50 for both is the classic ergonomic error: it designs for a person who does not exist and excludes half the population at each end.

envelopes.label: Older adult, ambulant
envelopes.gait_note: Reduced reach range in BOTH directions. The comfortable band narrows from roughly 400-1700 mm to 500-1500 mm, which is why storage designed for a younger body becomes unusable rather than merely inconvenient.

envelopes.label: Older adult with rollator
envelopes.note: Occupied depth includes the device in front of the body. This is why a rollator user needs more than a wheelchair user at a counter, not less.

envelopes.label: Manual wheelchair user
envelopes.note: The reach band 400-1200 mm is the single most useful number in accessible design. Anything a person must operate - switch, handle, socket, shelf, hob control - belongs inside it. Most standard kitchens put half their storage outside it.

envelopes.label: Care resident requiring assistance
envelopes.note: Reach is barely relevant: most tasks are performed BY someone else. The binding dimensions belong to the assisting staff, which is why staff_care must be modelled as a user group in its own right rather than folded in.

envelopes.label: Care staff at work
envelopes.note: A legally recognised user group in Sweden. Working space around a bed is an occupational-health requirement, not a comfort preference, and cannot be value-engineered away.

envelopes.label: Child, 3-5 years
envelopes.note: Eye height 970 mm sets vision panels and sill heights. The floor is a working surface at this age, which changes what a finish has to do.

activity_zones._note: The space an ACTIVITY occupies, not the object. This is the layer that turns furniture into a plan: a bed is 900x2000, but sleeping-and-getting-out-of-bed is considerably more, and only the second number tells you whether a room works.

zones.label: Stand and turn on the spot
Stand at an open wardrobe door
Seated at a table, chair pushed back to stand
Bending to a low oven or appliance
Making a bed from one side
Two staff assisting at a bed

turning._note: Manoeuvring space by device and level. Swedish practice distinguishes normalniva (dwellings) from hojd niva (raised level, public and care settings), which is why one number will not do.
